Juvenile Twobar seabream (Acanthopagrus bifasciatus) recruit to coastal nursery habitats along the Arabian Gulf and Sea of Oman, where they undergo a period of rapid somatic growth before attaining sexual maturity. Field surveys indicate that the standard length at which fifty percent of individuals reach puberty is 26.4 centimeters [Lp = 26.4 centimeters], a size typically achieved within the first two years of benthic life. This body length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 314 grams [Wwp = approximately 314 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain required for gonadal development and the initiation of vitellogenesis in females. At a stable water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of actively spawning individuals was estimated at 5% [GSI = 5%] during the spawning season. This index was derived from comparative data on congeneric sparids and confirms that reproductive investment in this species is comparable to that observed in other members of the Sparidae family inhabiting similar thermal regimes.

As Twobar seabream continue to grow beyond the pubertal threshold, they approach their ultimate standard length, which has been recorded at 36.2 centimeters [Li = 36.2 centimeters] in the oldest and largest individuals sampled from wild populations. This maximum linear dimension corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 818 grams [Wwi = 818 grams], a value that represents the upper asymptote of the weight-length relationship for this species. The allometric scaling between length and mass, derived from regression analyses of captured specimens, indicates that body mass increases disproportionately with length, a common pattern among teleosts with robust body forms. In contrast, the very earliest life stage—the recently fertilized ovum—presents a starkly different mass metric. Based on an average egg diameter of 750 micrometers, characteristic of the congener Acanthopagrus berda, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], illustrating the extreme ontogenetic range in body mass from the pelagic egg stage to the fully grown adult.

Longevity records for Twobar seabream indicate that individuals can reach a maximum lifespan of 8030 days [am = 8030 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], a thermal condition representative of their subtropical habitat. This extended lifespan—equivalent to roughly 22 years—positions this sparid among the longer-lived members of its genus, with age validation performed through otolith microstructure analysis. The relatively slow pace of senescence in this species is likely linked to the stable thermal conditions of its habitat, which minimize the metabolic costs associated with temperature extremes.

Comparative analysis of body size at different life stages reveals striking contrasts in the species' growth trajectory. Individuals begin their independent existence as minuscule larvae hatching from eggs weighing just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], a mass that underscores the vulnerability of early life stages to predation and starvation in the planktonic environment. From this minute starting point, juveniles undergo an exponential growth phase during which they accumulate somatic tissue rapidly, reaching a standard length of 26.4 centimeters [Lp = 26.4 centimeters] by the time they become sexually mature. At this pubertal stage, body mass has increased by over six orders of magnitude, achieving a wet weight at puberty of 314 grams [Wwp = 314 grams]. The energy allocation toward somatic growth during these formative years is prioritized over reproductive investment, a strategy that ensures individuals attain a body size sufficient to support the metabolic demands of gamete production and spawning migrations later in life.

The maximum achievable body dimensions of Twobar seabream are constrained by both genetic potential and ecological factors such as resource availability and intraspecific competition. The ultimate standard length of 36.2 centimeters [Li = 36.2 centimeters] represents the ceiling for linear growth under optimal conditions, while the asymptotic body mass of 818 grams [Wwi = 818 grams] defines the upper limit of somatic accumulation. These values align closely with predictions from length-weight regressions specific to the Sparidae family, which exhibit a characteristic exponent near 3.0. The gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] measured at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C] indicates that ovarian tissue accounted for about five percent of total body mass in spawning females. This moderate investment, combined with a maximum lifespan of 22 years [am = 22 years] under the same thermal conditions, suggests a life history strategy that balances current reproduction against future survival, a trade-off typical of long-lived, iteroparous marine fishes at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C].
